summary:
Kebbi stands under the national framework of Nigeria. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide and reaches well beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. The penalties apply to all persons present in the country, including visitors.

Sexual orientation and gender identity carry exposure at the border. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalising same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Kebbi runs its own religious criminal layer on top of that statute. Its Penal Code (Amendment) Law (Law No. 21 of 2000) was signed into law and came into operation on 1 December 2000, recorded in Kebbi State Gazette Vol. 2 No. 1, Supplement, 31 December 2000. The enacted text provides that whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm), while same-sex acts between women attract 50 lashes and imprisonment of up to six months. The UK Home Office note carries this as Kebbi's own row in its twelve-state Sharia penalties table at section 8.4.3, a dated government confirmation that Kebbi's code extends criminalisation to acts between women and is broader in scope and harsher in penalty than the federal statute for Muslim defendants.

Jurisdiction over that code is personal. Human Rights Watch (2004) records that by 2002 twelve northern states, Kebbi among them, had Shari'a criminal legislation and Sharia courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslims, and that these were the only states with such jurisdiction. A visitor who is Muslim, or is taken to be Muslim, therefore faces a religious court applying a penal code with a capital ceiling for men's acts; a visitor assessed as non-Muslim is not within that court's criminal jurisdiction, though the national statute still applies.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public, and whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here. Cross-dressing is separately penalised in some states, with Kano providing up to one year in prison or a fine for men who dress or behave as women and sentencing a TikToker to one year in prison in 2025.

Violence against trans people is documented and official response has been slow. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, the TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Police violence and extortion against perceived gay people are routine features of enforcement. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law producing a climate of hostility independent of its text. Visitors who use dating apps face a separate route to harm: the Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye). She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos and ending with release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
tangentialFactors:
Kebbi is one of twelve northern states that adopted Shari'a criminal legislation in the wave that followed Zamfara's re-adoption of criminal Shari'a (Shari'a Establishment Law enacted 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000). By 2002 the twelve states held the only Sharia courts in the country with criminal jurisdiction over Muslims, so the pattern Kebbi illustrates is regional rather than local.

The twelve-state bloc is not uniform in severity. Kaduna and Katsina share Kebbi's enacted wording of stoning to death for sodomy, while Wikipedia's account of the country places the capital maximum for lesbianism only in Kano and Katsina and puts most other states on an imprisonment or caning tier. Kebbi's own statute and that secondary account do not align on where the state sits, which is recorded as an unresolved point rather than settled here.

The cross-dressing layer is a separate axis from same-sex conduct and varies state by state, with Kano the most cited instance: up to one year in prison or a fine for men who dress or behave as women, and a 2025 one-year sentence against a TikToker. Kebbi's own provisions on gender expression are not documented in these sources.

Enforcement climate is shaped less by statutory text than by its use. The SSMPA is described by those affected as weaponised, producing hostility independent of its wording, and app-based luring by kito gangs gives visitors a specific, non-institutional route to assault and blackmail by threat of outing.
